course.learn: Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) is the system of certificates, keys, certificate authorities, policies, and validation mechanisms that creates scalable trust for public-key cryptography.
course.why: PKI lets systems verify that a public key belongs to the identity named in a certificate instead of trusting keys blindly.
course.example: A browser trusts a website certificate because it chains to a trusted CA and the certificate is valid for the site name and time period.
course.exam: Know CA, certificate, CSR, root/intermediate trust, revocation, CRL, and OCSP. PKI is about trust management, not just encryption.

slides.title: Type of Keys
slides.teach: Focus on the differences between the listed types and the clue words that distinguish them in exam questions.

course.learn: Cryptographic strength depends on using the correct key type, algorithm, key length, and exchange method. Keys must be generated, distributed, stored, rotated, and retired securely.
course.why: A strong algorithm can still fail if keys are weak, exposed, reused too long, or exchanged insecurely.
course.example: A server uses asymmetric cryptography to establish trust and exchange key material, then switches to fast symmetric encryption for the session.
course.exam: Focus on purpose: symmetric = fast shared secret; asymmetric = public/private pair; longer keys generally increase brute-force difficulty but algorithm choice also matters.

defs: A controlled arrangement where a copy of a cryptographic key is held by an authorized escrow agent for approved recovery scenarios.

course.learn: Key-management systems centralize the creation, storage, rotation, access, backup, and retirement of cryptographic keys. Key escrow stores a recoverable copy under controlled conditions.
course.why: Losing an encryption key can make legitimate data permanently inaccessible, while leaking the key destroys confidentiality.
course.example: A cloud KMS rotates database-encryption keys automatically and restricts key use to a specific application role.
course.exam: CompTIA may test availability versus confidentiality tradeoffs. Escrow improves recoverability but creates a high-value secret that must be strongly protected.
